title: The Mortgage Is Only the Cover Charge
meta_description: Calculate the true cost of owning a home: closing cash, taxes, insurance, repairs, HOA exposure, liquidity and realistic affordability shocks.

sections.heading: The Mortgage Is Only the Cover Charge
paragraphs: A mortgage quote answers a financing question: what principal and interest will this loan require under stated terms? It does not answer the household question: what will owning this property demand in cash, time and risk? Taxes, insurance, utilities, maintenance, association charges, closing costs and the loss of liquidity can turn an apparently comfortable payment into a fragile housing system. The home price is also not the final cost, because the building keeps sending invoices after closing.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau defines the total monthly home payment broadly: principal, interest, property taxes, mortgage insurance, homeowners insurance, supplementary coverage and association fees. [[S1|Its affordability guidance]] also warns that taxes and insurance can rise. This is why comparing rent with principal and interest alone is misleading. Rent bundles many ownership risks into one contractual payment, while a homeowner receives those risks separately and irregularly.

This article uses a transparent worked example: a $400,000 home, $40,000 down, a 30-year fixed mortgage, and illustrative annual property costs. It does not quote a current interest rate or claim affordability for any reader. Local taxes, insurance, HOA rules, climate exposure, building age and financing terms vary too widely. Replace every modeled amount with written estimates from the relevant property, lender, insurer, tax authority and inspection.

The objective is not to argue that renting is superior or ownership is a mistake. A home can provide stability, control, community attachment and long-term value. The objective is to buy enough margin with the house. If closing drains every reserve and the monthly plan has no repair contribution, the buyer has financed the visible asset while leaving its operating system unfunded.

Affordability therefore has three tests: cash to close without emptying emergency reserves; recurring all-in cost that leaves room for other goals; and capacity to absorb a plausible repair or insurance shock. Passing the lender's underwriting is not the same as passing all three. A lender evaluates loan repayment under its rules. The household must evaluate the life surrounding the loan.
Do not use the seller's monthly cost as the buyer's forecast. Financing, assessed value, insurance profile and exemptions can change at transfer. Build the new owner's numbers independently.

Separate affordability from approval before touring. Calculate the maximum all-in monthly amount that preserves retirement saving, emergency contributions and other essential goals, then subtract conservative estimates for non-mortgage property costs. The remainder—not the lender's headline approval—sets the principal-and-interest ceiling. This reverse calculation reduces the chance that enthusiasm for a particular property rewrites the budget after the household has already become emotionally committed.

Include time and physical capacity. Yard work, snow removal, project supervision and contractor access may require hours that were not part of renting. Outsourcing converts time into cash; doing it personally converts leisure and skill into maintenance. Neither is free, and disability, travel or caregiving can change the feasible mix after purchase.

sections.heading: Cash to Close Is More Than the Down Payment
paragraphs: The down payment receives attention because it changes the loan amount and may affect mortgage insurance. Closing brings a second stack: origination charges, appraisal, credit report, title services, recording or transfer charges, prepaid interest, initial insurance and escrow deposits, inspection and sometimes attorney or survey fees. The CFPB says closing costs typically range from 2 to 5 percent of purchase price, excluding the down payment, although actual costs vary. [[S1|That range]] makes a meaningful difference on a $400,000 property.

At 2 to 5 percent, the illustrative closing-cost range is $8,000 to $20,000 before moving, immediate repairs or furnishings. Adding a $40,000 down payment produces $48,000 to $60,000 due around purchase. A buyer arriving with exactly $40,000 does not have a ten-percent-down plan; the buyer has an incomplete cash plan that may require seller concessions, lender credits, a lower down payment or a delayed purchase.

Credits are not automatically free. A lender credit may be paired with a higher interest rate, and a seller concession may be reflected in negotiation or price. Rolling eligible costs into financing can spread the cash burden while increasing principal and long-term interest. Compare alternatives on the Loan Estimate and ask what changes in rate, payment and cash due. Solve the immediate constraint without hiding its later price.

Preserve three post-closing balances: an ordinary emergency fund, a dedicated home-repair reserve and cash for known first-year work. The inspection may identify an aging water heater that still functions, worn exterior paint or a roof with limited remaining life. Those are not surprises merely because the seller is not replacing them. Price and fund the condition before the keys arrive.

Include moving, utility deposits, locks, safety devices and basic tools. Avoid furnishing the entire home on credit during the first month. Empty rooms are visible and create pressure, but revolving debt can make the house unaffordable after the lender has already declared it affordable. Sequence purchases by safety and daily function, then learn how the space is actually used.
Request revised disclosures when loan terms change and compare them line by line. Urgency near closing is not a reason to stop asking what a fee purchases or whether it changed.

Keep proof for every cash source. Gift funds, sale proceeds and transferred savings may require documentation under loan rules, and moving money repeatedly near closing can create avoidable questions. Ask the lender what records are needed before consolidating funds. At the same time, do not place every liquid dollar into the transaction merely because it is documentable. The closing account and the post-closing reserve have different jobs.

Do not waive due diligence merely to make an offer more competitive without understanding the exposure. Inspection, financing, appraisal and document-review contingencies have legal and market-specific consequences. Use qualified local professionals to understand them. Winning a bid by accepting an unknown condition can be the most expensive form of certainty. Protect optionality until the important evidence has been reviewed and understood.

sections.heading: The Monthly Payment Has Several Moving Parts
paragraphs: Principal and interest may be fixed on a fixed-rate loan, but the total payment can still change. Escrow collections respond to tax bills and insurance premiums. Mortgage insurance may continue until eligibility and loan rules allow removal. HOA dues and special assessments usually sit outside the lender's advertised payment. Utilities depend on size, efficiency, climate and occupancy. Build the household budget from all-in housing cost, not the largest line on the mortgage statement.

Use a payment stack with separate rows for principal and interest, property tax, homeowners insurance, flood or other supplemental coverage, mortgage insurance, HOA dues, utilities and repair saving. For the worked model, suppose principal and interest are $2,275, taxes $500, insurance $200, mortgage insurance $150, HOA $100 and repair saving $400. Before utilities, the housing system costs $3,625, not $2,275.

The figures are illustrative, but the method prevents omission. A buyer focused on the mortgage would understate monthly housing by $1,350 in this example—more than half the quoted principal-and-interest payment. The gap is not discretionary simply because several bills are annual or escrowed. Dividing irregular charges into monthly equivalents reveals what the property consumes over time.

Read the Loan Estimate's projected payments and estimated taxes, insurance and assessments. Compare it with independent tax records, insurance quotes and association documents. An estimate is not a promise that costs remain constant. New construction tax assessments, expiring abatements or a purchase reassessment can change the bill after closing. Ask the tax authority how the property is assessed rather than relying only on the seller's historical payment.

Run the stack at today's amount and at stressed amounts. Increase taxes and insurance, add a plausible assessment and model a utility month at the high end. If the plan works only when every variable remains at its initial estimate, the property has no operating margin. Affordability should survive an ordinary unfavorable year, not only the disclosure's first page.
Escrow shortages can produce a temporary repayment amount on top of a permanently higher tax or premium. Read the annual analysis and separate the catch-up from the new baseline.

Compare payment stacks using the same assumptions. If one lender's worksheet excludes HOA dues or uses a lower tax estimate, correct it before judging that loan cheaper. Separate financing differences from property differences. Discount points, credits and adjustable features can shift cost across time, so evaluate cash today, payment under stated terms, break-even horizon and the consequence of selling or refinancing earlier than expected.

Utilities deserve property-specific estimates. Request available history, inspect fuel type and equipment, and model occupancy changes. A larger house can raise heating, cooling, water, cleaning and furnishing costs together. Efficiency upgrades may help, but savings estimates should include installation cost and actual usage rather than assuming every project pays for itself quickly.

sections.heading: Insurance Prices the Risk the Listing Does Not Show
paragraphs: Homeowners insurance is not a maintenance contract and does not cover every loss. Policies contain deductibles, exclusions, limits and valuation terms. Flood, earthquake, wind or other hazards may require separate coverage or carry different deductibles. Obtain property-specific quotes before contingencies expire where possible, and read the declarations and exclusions rather than budgeting from a national average.

Freddie Mac estimated that average annual homeowners insurance among its relevant borrowers rose from $1,081 in 2018 to $1,522 in 2023, a 40.8 percent increase. [[S2|Its analysis]] also found large geographic differences. That history does not forecast an individual's renewal, but it proves that a fixed mortgage rate does not freeze ownership cost. Insurance availability and price can become a property-selection issue.

Check disaster exposure using authoritative local and federal information, then ask the insurer what mitigation affects eligibility or premium. Roof age, electrical systems, plumbing, protective devices and building codes can matter. A cheap house with difficult coverage may not be cheap. A quote can also change after inspection, underwriting or renewal, so retain margin beyond the first premium.

Choose a deductible that the reserve can actually pay. A higher deductible may lower premium while transferring more loss to the household. If the homeowner cannot produce that amount after a covered event, the policy may protect the structure but leave repairs stalled. Match emergency cash and deductible instead of optimizing either in isolation.

Create a coverage inventory with photos, receipts for major items and secure copies of the policy. Understand replacement-cost versus actual-cash-value treatment where applicable and review limits after renovations. Insurance planning is administrative until a loss; then documentation, exclusions and cash access determine how quickly the home becomes functional again.

Insurance and inspection solve different problems. Inspection informs condition; insurance transfers specified losses. Neither guarantees that ordinary deterioration or every hazard will be paid by someone else.

Ask the insurer about replacement cost for the structure, not market value alone. Land value does not need reconstruction, while labor and materials can rise independently of sale prices. Ordinance or law coverage, water backup, service lines and valuable-property limits may matter depending on the home. The right coverage is property-specific; adding every endorsement blindly can waste money, while assuming a standard form covers every plausible loss can leave severe gaps.

Review insurance annually and after major work. Compare coverage as well as premium, notify the carrier when required and retain proof of mitigation. The cheapest renewal may increase deductibles or narrow terms. A policy that no longer matches rebuilding cost can leave a gap even when every premium was paid on time.

sections.heading: Maintenance Arrives as Systems, Not a Smooth Percentage
paragraphs: Rules of thumb such as one percent of home value can start a conversation but cannot inspect a roof. Maintenance depends on age, materials, climate, prior work, size and complexity. A newer condominium and an older detached house expose owners to different systems and association obligations. Build a component schedule: roof, HVAC, water heater, plumbing, electrical, appliances, exterior, drainage, windows and safety equipment.

For each component, record age, observed condition, expected remaining range, maintenance task and rough replacement estimate. The inspection is a snapshot, not a warranty, but it can populate this schedule. HUD's post-purchase counseling material emphasizes planning for systems including roofing, windows, insulation, electrical and HVAC. [[S3|That system approach]] is stronger than assuming average annual spending will arrive evenly.

Separate routine maintenance, foreseeable replacement and true emergency repair. Gutter cleaning is routine. An old water heater is a foreseeable replacement even if the date is unknown. A burst supply line is an emergency. Fund all three differently: monthly operating money, sinking funds for aging systems, and accessible emergency cash for sudden damage. Combining them creates the illusion of one large reserve while known claims already own much of it.

Use ranges rather than false precision. Contractor availability, permits and hidden damage can change a quote. Include temporary lodging or lost work when a repair can make the home unusable. A $10,000 equipment estimate may require more cash if electrical upgrades or demolition are discovered. Contingency belongs in repair planning, not only construction television.

Preventive work competes with visible upgrades, which is why it is easily postponed. The new kitchen can be photographed; drainage correction cannot. Rank work by safety, water control, structure, mechanical reliability and efficiency before aesthetics. Water intrusion and deferred exterior work can turn a manageable task into a larger claim that insurance may not cover as ordinary neglect.

A maintenance calendar should include inexpensive tasks that preserve safety, such as detector testing and filter changes. Small recurring work protects both systems and the reserve intended for larger failures.

Create a first-year maintenance map before choosing cosmetic projects. Schedule inspection follow-ups, seasonal servicing, drainage checks and safety corrections. Obtain specialist evaluations where the general inspection recommends them. If several systems are near the end of expected life, do not average their costs over decades; the household may face a replacement cluster soon after purchase. Timing concentration is as important as lifetime average.

Create contractor-selection rules before an emergency: verify licensing where applicable, insurance, written scope, payment schedule and permits; obtain comparisons when time permits; and distrust pressure for full cash payment upfront. Preparation cannot remove repair stress, but it can reduce the chance that urgency produces a second financial problem.

sections.heading: Association Dues Are Not the Association Cost
paragraphs: Condominiums, townhomes and planned communities add a second financial system. Regular dues fund stated operations, but reserves and governance determine whether the association can handle major work. Review budgets, reserve studies, financial statements, insurance, meeting minutes, litigation and planned assessments within the legal review period. A low monthly due can reflect efficiency or underfunding; the number alone cannot distinguish them.

Ask what the association maintains and what the owner maintains. Windows, roofs, pipes, balconies and exterior surfaces can fall on different sides of the boundary. Compare the master policy with the unit owner's coverage and loss-assessment protection. An owner can face both personal deductibles and a share of association costs after damage.

Special assessments are lumpy ownership costs. HUD housing-counselor material notes that upcoming assessments may be announced in advance and should be saved for, and that unpaid HOA obligations can lead to serious consequences. [[S3|The guidance]] reinforces why association documents belong in affordability analysis rather than being treated as background paperwork.

Stress the association scenario with a plausible assessment and dues increase. If a $10,000 assessment would require high-cost debt, the buyer needs more reserve or a different property. Financing options sometimes exist, but they do not erase the liability. The building's deferred maintenance can become the unit owner's debt without appearing in the mortgage approval.

Governance has a time cost too. Owners may need to attend meetings, review proposals and vote on expensive projects. Poor participation can leave decisions to a small group; conflict can delay necessary repairs. This is part of ownership, especially where common systems are substantial. The purchase includes a share of an organization, not only rooms behind a door.

For a self-managed property without an association, the owner still has governance duties: permits, boundaries, local rules and contractor decisions. Absence of dues does not mean absence of administration.

Read association documents for delinquency, owner concentration and insurance deductibles as well as the reserve balance. A healthy-looking account can still be inadequate relative to planned projects, and a high delinquency rate can shift pressure to paying owners. Confirm rental restrictions and pending rule changes when flexibility matters. Legal review may be valuable because bylaws, declarations and local statutes determine obligations that a marketing summary cannot override.

For associations, ask whether major components have been inspected and whether reserve assumptions match current bids. Inflation can make an old reserve study optimistic. Meeting minutes may reveal repeated deferrals, owner disputes or insurance changes that the balance sheet alone misses. The cheapest unit can be attached to the most expensive unresolved building problem.

sections.heading: Equity Is Real, but It Is Not a Checking Account
paragraphs: Mortgage principal payments can build equity, and appreciation can add value, but neither guarantees accessible cash. Selling requires time and transaction costs. Borrowing against equity adds a lien, qualification, interest and payment. A household can be wealthy on paper and unable to pay a furnace invoice without debt. Keep liquidity in the affordability test rather than assuming the house can fund itself.

The down payment also has an opportunity cost. Cash invested in the property cannot simultaneously remain in diversified investments or an emergency account. That does not make the down payment a loss; it means the choice has alternatives. Compare ownership benefits with the return, liquidity and flexibility surrendered, using conservative assumptions rather than guaranteed appreciation.

Principal is not the whole payment. Interest, taxes, insurance, maintenance and many transaction costs do not become equity. Some may support the home's use or protect value, but they should not be described as saving. This distinction makes rent-versus-buy analysis more honest: rent is not uniquely 'throwing money away,' and ownership is not uniquely converting every housing dollar into wealth.

Transaction costs make holding period important. Closing expenses arrive at purchase; selling can bring commissions, taxes, repairs and concessions. A person expecting relocation in a short period faces more risk that costs overwhelm appreciation and principal reduction. Flexibility has financial value, especially when career or family plans are uncertain.

Do not drain retirement accounts casually for the purchase. Taxes, penalties, lost compounding and plan rules can make the long-term cost much larger than the cash received. Evaluate permitted options with qualified tax and financial guidance. A bigger down payment is not automatically stronger if it weakens every other layer of the household balance sheet.
Home equity should be reported beside mortgage balance and accessible reserves, not combined with them. Separate columns prevent a rising estimate from disguising weak cash protection.

Do not count estimated appreciation as income in the monthly plan. Appreciation does not pay taxes, maintenance or insurance unless the owner sells or borrows, each with cost and uncertainty. Similarly, an interest deduction should not be treated as a guaranteed rebate; eligibility and benefit depend on current tax law and the household's filing circumstances. Affordability must work before uncertain tax or price benefits.

Track net sale proceeds, not an online value estimate. Subtract mortgage payoff, selling costs, taxes where applicable, repairs and concessions. This prevents a paper gain from being treated as immediately available wealth. Equity remains useful, but planning should respect the steps and costs required to convert it into cash.

sections.heading: Rent Versus Buy Is a Scenario, Not a Slogan
paragraphs: Compare equivalent housing and time horizons. A small apartment and a detached house provide different space, maintenance and location; comparing their payments answers a lifestyle question, not only a tenure question. Include renter insurance, likely rent changes and moving costs on one side; include all ownership costs, purchase and sale friction and repair risk on the other.

Model several home-price and rent paths rather than one confident forecast. Appreciation may be strong, flat or negative over the relevant period. Investment returns are uncertain too. The result should be a range showing what assumptions drive the decision. If buying wins only with rapid appreciation, the plan is a leveraged price bet dressed as housing certainty.

Value nonfinancial benefits explicitly. Stability, control over the space, pets, schools and community ties may justify a higher expected cost. Renting can offer mobility, fewer repair responsibilities and preserved liquidity. These are not excuses that contaminate the math; they are benefits being purchased. Naming them prevents the calculation from pretending that money is the only outcome.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported housing as 33.4 percent of average consumer-unit expenditure in 2024, the largest major category. [[S4|The average]] is not an affordability threshold, but it shows why a housing error affects the whole plan. Overbuying can crowd out retirement, childcare, transport, healthcare and the ability to handle income interruption.

Delay is a valid result. A buyer can improve credit, increase reserves, research neighborhoods or wait for job stability without predicting prices. Buying later may cost more or less; certainty is unavailable. The decision to wait can still be correct when today's purchase would eliminate margin. Readiness is partly the ability to survive ownership after winning the bid.

A rent-versus-buy spreadsheet should disclose its selling-cost, appreciation, investment-return and holding-period assumptions. Hidden assumptions create confident answers rather than useful decisions.

Run the renter scenario with a renter's investment discipline rather than assuming every avoided ownership dollar disappears. Run the owner scenario without pretending every renter would invest perfectly. The comparison should illuminate sensitivity, not manufacture a winner through biased behavior assumptions. When results are close, lifestyle fit, risk tolerance and expected mobility may properly decide. Precision in the spreadsheet cannot eliminate uncertainty in the future.

If either scenario depends on staying a specific number of years, write that break-even assumption beside career and family plans. A spreadsheet cannot force the household to remain after job loss, divorce, health change or caregiving need. Flexibility deserves a larger weight when life plans are genuinely unsettled.

sections.heading: Use the Property Ledger Before Making an Offer
paragraphs: Build a one-page property ledger for every serious candidate. List cash to close, post-closing reserves, total monthly payment, utilities, maintenance contribution, known system replacements, insurance deductibles, association exposure and commute changes. Attach sources and dates. This turns vague affordability into a comparable record and prevents emotional attachment from selectively forgetting an expense.

Run four shocks: insurance rises 25 percent, taxes rise 15 percent, a $10,000 repair occurs, and one income falls for three months. These are tests, not forecasts. Decide which resources cover each shock and whether using them damages another essential goal. If the answer is credit cards for every scenario, the house needs a lower price, larger reserve or different timing.

Set a bid ceiling from the all-in ledger before negotiation. Do not raise it because the monthly principal-and-interest difference appears small. A higher price also affects down payment, closing cash, taxes, insurance, mortgage insurance and future transaction costs. The ceiling protects the system, not the ego of winning.

After purchase, keep the ledger alive. Review insurance at renewal, property tax notices, escrow analysis, system ages and association documents. Transfer a monthly amount to home reserves. Record completed maintenance and warranties. Ownership becomes less surprising when the house is managed as a collection of systems rather than one automatic mortgage payment.

The right home is not the maximum property a lender will finance. It is a property whose full cost can coexist with emergency savings, retirement, daily life and uncertainty. The mortgage opens the door. The household must still afford everything that keeps the door, roof, pipes, insurance and future choices intact.
Walk away when documentation is incomplete or the ledger requires optimistic guesses. Another property may appear; cash lost to an unexamined risk is harder to replace.

Bring the ledger to the inspection, insurance call and final walkthrough. Update condition, quotes and seller credits as facts change. Verify agreed repairs and confirm major systems operate; the walkthrough is not a second full inspection, but it can catch damage or missing items before transfer. Keep the ledger after closing so the first tax notice, escrow analysis or repair quote improves the plan instead of arriving without context.

The final ceiling should include a stop rule. If insurance, inspection or association facts push the all-in cost beyond the ceiling, renegotiate or walk away. A ceiling that moves whenever new risk appears is not a constraint. Protecting the household after an expensive investigation is more valuable than completing the transaction to justify sunk effort.

summary: A mortgage quote is not the cost of owning a home. The all-in system includes principal, interest, property taxes, homeowners and supplemental insurance, mortgage insurance, association dues, utilities, maintenance, repairs and transaction costs. A fixed-rate mortgage can still produce a rising total payment when escrowed taxes and premiums change.

Cash to close includes more than the down payment. CFPB guidance places typical closing costs around 2 to 5 percent of purchase price, though actual costs vary. A $400,000 worked example therefore adds roughly $8,000 to $20,000 before moving and first-year work. Preserve emergency, repair and known-project reserves after closing rather than arriving with an empty account.

Construct a monthly payment stack. In the illustrative case, $2,275 of principal and interest becomes $3,625 before utilities after adding taxes, insurance, mortgage insurance, HOA dues and repair saving. Replace those numbers with property-specific records. Stress taxes, insurance, assessments and utilities instead of assuming first-year estimates remain fixed.

Insurance prices risks the listing may not show. Obtain property-specific quotes, investigate hazard exposure, read deductibles and exclusions, and hold enough cash to pay the deductible. Insurance does not replace maintenance. An inspection informs condition but is not a warranty, and neither tool guarantees every loss will be covered.

Manage maintenance by building system rather than one smooth percentage. Record roof, HVAC, water heater, plumbing, electrical, exterior and appliance ages and condition. Separate routine work, foreseeable replacement and emergency repair. Fund them with operating money, sinking funds and emergency cash respectively, and prioritize safety, water control and structure before cosmetic upgrades.

Association ownership adds governance and assessment risk. Review reserves, budgets, minutes, insurance, litigation and planned projects. Confirm what the association and unit owner each maintain. A low monthly due can conceal underfunding, while an assessment can become the owner's debt without ever appearing in mortgage approval.

Equity is valuable but not liquid. Selling takes time and costs money; borrowing adds interest and a payment. Principal builds equity, while interest, taxes, insurance and most maintenance do not. Rent-versus-buy comparisons should use equivalent housing, multiple price paths, transaction costs and an honest holding period while valuing stability and flexibility explicitly.

Before offering, create a property ledger covering cash to close, post-closing reserves, total monthly cost, system replacements, deductibles and association exposure. Test an insurance increase, tax increase, major repair and temporary income loss. Set the bid ceiling from the all-in ledger. The right home is the one that leaves the rest of the household financially functional.

Calculate the principal-and-interest ceiling by starting with the household's affordable all-in amount and subtracting conservative taxes, insurance, dues, utilities and repair funding. This reverses the common process of accepting a loan approval and trying to squeeze every other cost beneath it. Preserve emergency saving, retirement and essential goals before selecting the house price.

Use the same assumptions when comparing lenders and properties. Correct missing HOA charges or unrealistic tax estimates, and evaluate points or credits across the expected holding period. Keep uncertain appreciation and tax benefits outside the survival budget. They may improve the outcome, but the household should not need them to make ordinary ownership work.

Update the property ledger through inspection, insurance quotes, final disclosures and walkthrough. After closing, record tax notices, escrow changes, system work and warranties. A living ledger turns each new fact into planning information. The mortgage opens the transaction, but reserves, maintenance and ongoing administration determine whether ownership remains stable.

Include a stop rule. When inspection, insurance or association evidence pushes the all-in cost beyond the preset ceiling, renegotiate or leave. Do not let money already spent on appraisal or inspection justify a larger future loss. Due diligence is valuable when it gives the buyer permission to say no.

faq.question: What should be included in an all-in housing payment?
faq.answer: Include principal, interest, taxes, homeowners and supplemental insurance, mortgage insurance, HOA dues, utilities and a realistic maintenance contribution.

faq.question: How much are closing costs?
faq.answer: CFPB guidance says they typically range from 2 to 5 percent of purchase price excluding the down payment, but actual charges depend on the loan, property and location.

faq.question: Is a home inspection a warranty?
faq.answer: No. It is a condition assessment within the inspection scope and time available. Use it to plan further evaluation, negotiation and future system costs.

faq.question: Does homeowners insurance cover maintenance?
faq.answer: Generally no. Policies cover specified losses subject to terms, limits, exclusions and deductibles; ordinary wear, deterioration and many maintenance failures are not insurance substitutes.

faq.question: How should buyers plan for HOA assessments?
faq.answer: Review reserve studies, budgets, minutes and planned projects, then stress-test a plausible assessment and keep adequate liquidity or choose a different property.

faq.question: Is paying a mortgage always better than renting?
faq.answer: No. Compare equivalent housing, all ownership and rental costs, holding period, transaction costs, uncertain returns and the value of stability or flexibility.

glossary.definition: The loan repayment and financing charge portions of a mortgage payment.
Funds collected by a servicer to pay specified property taxes and insurance when due.
Loan and transaction charges paid around completion of a home purchase.
Coverage protecting the lender against specified borrower default risk.
An additional association charge for expenses not covered by regular dues and reserves.
Cash accumulated for foreseeable major home-system replacement.
The amount a policyholder bears before covered insurance payment applies.
The value of the best alternative use of money committed to the property.
The length of time the buyer expects to own before selling.
A consolidated record of acquisition cash, recurring costs, reserves, risks and system condition.
